catalog_locator: Vesalainen 2016, ch. 2 Phonology: sec. 2.2 Vowels, printed p. 5 (PDF p. 24) incl. footnote 1, and sec. 2.3 Tone, printed p. 6 (PDF p. 25) incl. footnote 2; Watters 2002, sec. 6.2 'Syllable tone (Dzongkha and Lhomi)', printed pp. 40 and 43 (scanned text, 1572-1576) and sec. 6.3 Summary, printed p. 44 (scanned).
catalog_quote: A Lhomi word is either a high register word or a low register word. This means that the phonation of the vowels is either clear or breathy. This is the salient feature of Lhomi tonology. ... I argue that it is the vowel quality (tense/lax) that is contrastive, not the pitch. High register (tense) words are also more stressed than the low register ones (word stress). These observations need to be either confirmed or refuted by a detailed study. ... He notes that “vowel length is contrastive on the first syllable of disyllabic words, but not on the second syllable. It may be that when the first syllable of a disyllabic word is long it attracts stress, or that the lengthening of the syllable results from its being stressed.” (Ibid., 254). [fn. 2:] I would like to argue for the first option without giving any concrete evidence at this point. [Watters 2002:40:] Vowel length is contrastive on the first syllable of disyllabic words, but not on the second syllable. When the first syllable is long it attracts stress, or perhaps it is because this syllable is stressed that it is lengthened. In any case, this syllable is “heavy” in comparison to the one which follows it. When the first syllable is short, the first and second syllables seem to be of equal “weight” in terms of quantity and “stress.”
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lhomi is described as a two-register (high/tense-clear vs low/lax-breathy) tone language in which word stress is a correlate rather than an independent contrastive position: high-register words are said to be 'more stressed' than low-register words, and in disyllabic words a long first syllable is heavy and attracts stress (Watters 2002:40 adds that when the first syllable is short both syllables are of roughly equal weight and stress). No fixed-position rule is stated by either source; the stress claims are explicitly hedged as awaiting a detailed study.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; Vesalainen notes 'phonological stress' on the negative prefix (p. 130) and on final question clitics (pp. 139-140, 234), which is emphatic/pragmatic prominence, not a lexical rule. Watters 2002:43-44 says pitch/stress on words like 'moon' vs 'monkey' is not predictable from onset phonation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (mono- and disyllabic citation forms, elicited from Chepuwa-village Lhomi in Vesalainen; Watters 2002 used ~1,000 recorded words from several speakers, Sankhuwa Sabha). Watters 2002 (pp. 40, 43) is the first-hand instrumental basis; Vesalainen 2016 explicitly defers to Watters and adds the register-stress observation.
new_statements.identity_note: Vesalainen's grammar describes the Chepuwa-village dialect of Lhomi (Sankhuwasabha district, Nepal), the reference variety for lhom1239; Watters 2002/2003 describes Lhomi of Sankhuwa Sabha near the Nepal-China border without naming a village. No other variety involved. Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 classify Lhomi as group 68.1 with Thudam (thud1238, now merged into Walungge [ola]) as 68.2.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lhomi words carry a register contrast (clear vs breathy phonation, high vs low); high-register words are said to be 'more stressed' than low-register ones. The only positional remark is secondhand (Watters 2003): a long first syllable of a disyllabic word attracts stress, which the author endorses tentatively. No general word-stress placement rule is stated; the author says the claims are unconfirmed.
new_statements.exceptions: None as a stress rule. Elsewhere the sketch notes 'phonological stress' on the negative prefix (p. 167) and on final question clitics (pp. 126, 178, 179, 251), i.e. emphatic/pragmatic prominence on grammatical morphemes, not lexical word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Vesalainen's sketch describes the Lhomi of Chepuwa village, Sankhuwa Sabha (upper Arun), per the 2016 edition p. 3; Watters places Lhomi in Sankhuwa Sabha near the Nepal-China border. Both are lhom1239.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (tonal: tense/lax register words with pitch contours, as in Vesalainen 2016 sec. 2.3); silent on the catalog's stress remark ('high register (tense) words are also more stressed') and on Watters' first-syllable length/stress observation. new_statements.rule_in_words: A clause-level syntax monograph (tagmemic nine-cell analysis). Its only phonological content is note 1: a consonant and vowel inventory and a key to four tone marks combining a tense vs lax register with a rising vs non-rising pitch contour, i.e. Lhomi is written as a register-tone language. Nothing is said about word stress, accent placement, or syllable weight.
new_statements.identity_note: PL B-53 note 1: Lhomi of the Upper Arun Valley, Sankhuwa Sabha district, Kosi zone, East Nepal; data 'represents the dialect spoken in Chepuwa' (fieldwork July 1975 - May 1976), the same village dialect as Vesalainen 2014/2016 = lhom1239.
